posts.text:
💻 🛑 After the PHP flaw, who in football is running PHP?
I scanned the official websites of all 96 clubs in Europe’s top five leagues, from the front door only. Here is the map.

On Wednesday a PHP vulnerability was in the news worldwide, two flaws in the language that runs most of the web, found this summer by research teams working with AI models. Everyone covered the flaw. I wanted to know whether it touches our corner of the world, so I pointed my YouTube Football Tracker at the 96 club sites it already stores and read what each home page tells any visitor: headers, cookies, the fingerprints a CMS leaves behind. One passive request per club, no probing, and a lot of reading page source by hand where the script fell short. This tells you the stack, never whether a site is patched. Hold that distinction.

What the scan found, 23 October 2026:
🔴 35 of 96 club sites run PHP, 36%. Three of those are inferred, so the declared figure is 32.
🟢 61 run a non-PHP stack I could name. No site was left unknown.
🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Premier League: 0 of 20 on PHP, and 12 of 20 sit on two shared platforms.
🇮🇹 Serie A: 10 of 20.
🇫🇷 Ligue 1: 13 of 18.
🇪🇸 La Liga and 🇩🇪 Bundesliga: 6 each.
🛡️ 63 of 96 sit behind a CDN or WAF.
🌐 33 expose their origin directly.
📝 WordPress is the most common CMS, 16 of 96.
⚙️ Next.js is the most common framework, 28 of 96.
⚠️ The sharp end: 21 clubs run PHP with nothing in front of the origin. I am not naming them.

🤖 My take: probably no major drama this time.
The patch is out, the big hosts and CDNs moved before most of us read the headline, and for a club the job is the boring one, update your versions and keep them updated.
The exposure in European club football sits in Italy and France, while the Premier League has a different risk, a dozen clubs on two vendors, so one bad day at a vendor is a bad day for half the league. And a bug that sat in PHP for ten years was pulled out by people pointing AI models at the source, and those tools are now in everyone’s hands, including people who will never file a responsible disclosure.
If this is the first of many AI-discovered vulnerabilities, how long can a club site stay one version behind?

Full method, charts and the caveats in the article below.

A guy with a scarf - Ep. 60: Stephen Tallent
“That integration layer is basically everything. That is the duct tape that’s holding up these apps.”
This is the second clip from my conversation with Stephen Tallent, CEO of Mercury Intermedia and the architect of Quicksilver Stream, and it’s the bit of the episode I keep coming back to, because it describes the part of a streaming service that eats time and budget long after launch day.

Stephen’s team kept building the same thing for customer after customer, the layer that sits between the apps on Roku, Apple TV, connected TV, mobile and web and all the systems running behind them. He doesn’t blame the platforms those customers picked, and Mercury is fully in favour of buying a platform instead of building one from scratch, but every platform hits a wall somewhere and someone has to write the code that gets around it. After enough projects the approach started to look the same every time, one back end that every device talks to, orchestrating a lot of different systems underneath, and Quicksilver Stream came out of those repeated patterns.

I like products that are born this way, from work done over and over on real client projects, because the problem they solve has already been paid for by somebody. I advise Mercury on Quicksilver Stream, so read this as an interestied view.

If your apps are held together by integrations that have been rewritten more than once, have a look at Quicksilver Stream, or send me a message and I’ll put you in touch with Stephen and the team.

Tom Richardson Mike Ligon Rusty Mitchell William J. (Bill) Tallent

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
🔟 10 Things To Consider about the Two Circles Fan Economy 2026 report
What the report says, where I agree, and why five ten-year-olds in Turin make me doubt the word "ownership"

Two Circles have put a number on fandom, $1.94tn in 2025. I worked with them on NFL Game Pass International, under the same investor, so I read it with respect and with a fair idea of what it is designed to do.

💰 1. The size. $1.94tn, close to 2% of global output. Sports and entertainment together, no split for sport.
📈 2. The growth. About 6% a year since 2010 against 3.8% for global GDP, on 5.8bn fans.
🙋 3. Fandom as the higher choice. Trust in institutions falls since 2005, identity shaped by fandom passes 90%.
📺 4. Media, advertisers and capital follow. 96 of the 100 most watched US broadcasts in 2025 were live sport, $570bn a year of marketing spend, the $55bn EA take-private.
🧩 5. Three layers around the fan. Interfaces and infrastructure, attention aggregators, IP owners. Sports IP revenue at a record $174bn in 2025.
🤝 6. Positive-sum economics. Consuming fandom creates more demand: Apple and Netflix sharing F1, ESPN and FOX One, the BBC and Sidemen watchalong.
🔁 7. Fan marketing runs on existing fans. 80% of value from existing customers, half of it in fewer than 5% of operating days. Loyalty ahead of penetration.
🎯 8. Moments and inside-out creative. Plan around fixtures and drops, join conversations fans already have, build from their rituals.
🏢 9. Four case studies. EA Advertising, Google in product partnerships, PL+ in Singapore, Disney moving to lifetime value per fan.
📘 10. The playbook. Seven imperatives under "know fans best", which is also the Two Circles tagline, mapped onto their own services on the last page.

😎 My take.
Nobody owns a fan.
The first half draws a market where value comes from collaboration across layers, and by page fourteen the Premier League is "taking ownership of the fan value chain". Companies own rights, data, billing relationships and access points. The attachment belongs to the fan, who can cancel, switch, pirate or simply stop caring on a Tuesday.
Earlier this year I interviewed five ten-year-old teammates of my son for "Football Through Their Eyes". Their football lives on the pitch, on live TV, on the PlayStation, in the Panini album and in arguments with friends, and the memory that mattered most to all five was a match they played themselves.
A designed journey beats disconnected touchpoints, and I have built both. Fans still pick their own path through whatever you designed, and the companies that grow know which role they play in that ecosystem.
Two Circles drew the ecosystem well. I would like the second half of the report to trust the first.

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
🎙️ Ep. 61 of A guy with a scarf is out, with Julie Neenan Souza Souza, six years Global Head of Sports at Amazon Web Services (AWS) and now Executive in Residence at PwC.
Julie is someone I wanted on the show for a long time. While she carried the AWS badge it was never the right moment, and it got easier once she stepped away, which turned out to be the better version anyway, because the conversation went where it wanted to go, from a scrappy college sports startup to whether AI is making the next generation duller. We crossed paths at a lot of events over those years and I always admired the energy, and that on stage she brought her whole self, humour and opinions included, which is rare for someone carrying a badge that size.

Key points and quotes:
🪣 The three-bucket test for any technology project: the business problem, the solution deployed, and the outcome with a number on it. "If we can't explain it in three big buckets, then there's not a story there."
🕶️ The metaverse locker room a team asked AWS to build, and her first question: "Why do you want to do that?" She is seeing "we want an AI strategy" land in exactly the same shape now.
⏳ On measuring too early: "If you're looking for quick wins, you might have a few of those, but I don't think then you're using it to its full power either." The NFL kickoff rule was run through 10,000 simulated seasons before it changed.
🏈 "When I was at AWS, I wanted the big thorny problems."
🤝 On who should hold a multi-vendor solution together: "You want somebody you trust quarterbacking that." And on doing it all in-house: "If anybody's telling you they can do it all, that's probably not true."
🏁 On the argument that regulation means falling behind in the global race: "What are we racing toward? Like human extinction? Because I'm fine falling behind on that."
🧠 On AI and junior jobs: "How you know to make high judgment decisions is through experience." Stanford's August 2026 data has 22 to 25 year olds in AI-exposed jobs 19% behind their peers, with no gap for experienced workers.
🥱 On offloading your thinking to an agent: "I think you're going to be a more boring person."
🏟️ "I don't think live sports can be disintermediated."
And boy do I agree with that!!!

Full conversation in the video, companion article below.

posts.text:
⚽ The season on YouTube so far: 106 days
Since 1 July the 101 club and league channels of Europe’s five big leagues have published 21,001 videos and collected 2.86 billion views. I took the YouTube Football Tracker’s season dashboards apart one chart at a time, for all five leagues together and for each league on its own, and published the six pages on my research hub.

📊 All five leagues
The Premier League has 1.1 billion views from 4,287 videos, La Liga 920 million from 6,626, so the league that publishes most earns second most, and an English upload is worth three and a half times an Italian one. Shorts carry every league, from 59% of views in England to 75% in France, and the shortest Shorts and the shortest long-form clips earn the most per video everywhere.
🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 The Premier League
The league channel sets the pace with Shorts that average close to a million views, Manchester City owns long-form at 745 thousand a video, and the five most consistent channels are the five biggest. A Brighton Short with 6.3 million views and 35 comments asks a question of its own.
🇪🇸 LALIGA
Barcelona and Real Madrid take 58% of the views, the league channel owns long-form, and Sevilla gets 96% of its views from Shorts. One Alavés Short is 79% of the club’s season, and Rayo Vallecano has published 22 videos in 106 days.
🇩🇪 Bundesliga
Bayern takes almost half of all Bundesliga views from fewer videos than the league channel, the clubs stream more than any other league and get the least for it, and the biggest video of the season is a referee’s microphone. The smaller clubs win on engagement, publish on the night and vanish for weeks at a time.
🇮🇹 Lega Serie A
Juventus sets the pace on Shorts, the league channel owns long-form, Inter publishes more than anyone and gets less per video, and Napoli goes silent for most of the season. One Como Short is the only one-hit wonder in the whole league.
🇫🇷 Ligue 1
PSG takes 70% of the views and the whole of the top eleven, with one eight-second Short at 44 million views, the league channel owns long-form, and nine clubs are silent on more than half the days of the season.

👉 All six pages: https://lnkd.in/dNUg7YHp

📺 The data comes from the YouTube Football Tracker, which follows more than 100 club and league channels every night.
 ⚽ If you run social for a club or a league, it shows you what your rivals publish, when and in which format, and which of their videos actually travel.
 ✒️ If you are a sports journalist, it shows you which stories, clubs and formats are working on YouTube this week, with the numbers to back the piece.
🔗 https://lnkd.in/dTQqMGYJ

this is nice but if you are serious about directly growing your YouTube channel look no further then BuzzMyVideos and chat with my friends Paola Marinone and Bengu Atamer

Euroleague Basketball is hiring a Streaming & Media Technology Director in Barcelona, which I spotted in David Cushnan's Leaders newsletter, and I'm sharing it because a few of the tech and ops people in my network could do this job well.

You'd own EuroLeague TV from ingest and encoding through CDN, DRM and playback, plus the media asset management, the automated content stack, the archive, content protection, geo-blocking and entitlements, onboarding of third-party content, distribution to partner platforms and the game-night incident process, with nobody reporting to you and the commercial side of partner deals handled by someone else.
If one of you gets the job, you owe me a dinner in Barcelona.
https://lnkd.in/dRdV3FCN

P.S.
A note for whoever wrote the posting, with respect, because the role is described in a lot of detail. One of the requirements is being able to write clear technical requirements and then check what vendors deliver against them, so I read the page that way and couldn't find anything on Euroleague's side: no salary range, no package, no benefits, no word on hybrid, and the page goes from "Your mission" and "Your profile" straight to "About us". That's twenty bullets of responsibilities for a Director role and nothing about what you get back, and the good candidates will ask about that in the first call anyway.

📺📲 Dolby OptiView at IBC 2026, three interviews and one booth tour.

I spent three days on the stand in Hall 5 with a microphone and a camera, and this is what the company brought to Amsterdam, in the order the demos ran:
🧠 Sports Intelligence, new. Two halves: content intelligence scores every moment of a game for excitement and cuts the clips, viewer intelligence reads the audience and predicts, minute by minute, when a fan is about to leave.
📺 Dolby OptiView Ads cut loose from the player. It now ships as an SDK that works with any player, so you keep what you run and add the ads piece.
🤝 Google Ad Manager certification, which Dolby’s release calls the first server-guided ad insertion solution verified within the Google ecosystem. Dolby’s own figure from one deployment: 76% average eCPM lift, 132% average fill-rate lift.
🎨 Dolby Vision through Dolby OptiView for the first time, with one-button up-conversion for the SDR productions that still make up most of live sport. The Seattle Seahawks are first.
⏱️ Latency as a setting, with synchronised playback across the audience.

The three people who built it walked me through it on camera:
🎙️ Giles Baker, SVP Dolby Cloud Solutions, on the strategy and the three-year view
 🎙️ Dan Coffey, Director of Product, on the portfolio and the clipping demo, recorded at 8am because the day before the booth was too crowded to film in
 🎙️ Paul Boustead, VP of Product Strategy, on exit risk and the case for lean-back personalisation

I also wrote down what I would push back on, because a sponsored stand is a captive audience and the questions a buyer should ask are harder than the ones I asked on camera.
👇 Full write-up, with all three videos embedded below.

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
Netflix has bought the 2030 World Cup for Spain and Andorra, announced today with FIFA, and it will stream all 104 matches live, with one match per matchday free and a package with every Spain game, both semi-finals and the final going to a Spanish free-to-air channel that hasn’t been named yet.

I started in this business in 1987 and I have lost count of the times we said a streamer would never buy the biggest tournament in the world, in a country where football sits next to religion, and we said it with the same confidence we used for “nobody will watch a full match on a phone”. It happened anyway, the way most of those things happened, and it has a name, it’s called transformation.

Maybe Netflix is buying events and leaving league seasons to others, so the Serie A and Ligue 1 tenders he expects in the coming months probably won’t get a Netflix bid.
The free-to-air channel that gets the Spain package will be buying the national team from Netflix, and Netflix now decides what Spanish fans see for free during a home World Cup, which is a big shift for the Spanish TV market.

posts.text:
🛑 STOP Making This Mistake with Your API Strategy
I am sharing this because it truly resonates with my direct experience in streaming as a B2B vendor.

📺 Any streaming service that reaches some scale ends up living on a long list of devices, web, iOS, Android, Apple TV, Android TV, Fire TV, Roku, Samsung, LG, and the list grows with every distribution deal. Each of those apps is often built by a different team or partner, sometimes in a different language, and each one tends to carry its own copy of the rules the business runs on: who is entitled to what, which offer appears where, what happens when a subscription lapses, how a geo restriction applies to a given match. Those copies drift apart over time, so a fix lands on one platform weeks before it reaches another, and the product team spends a lot of its energy keeping ten apps in agreement with each other.

In the first clip from my conversation with Stephen Tallent, CEO of Mercury Intermedia, he goes straight at this:

 ⚙️ "So we feel it's pretty important to plan from the beginning to have all your platforms talking to the same APIs and provide as much of the business logic as possible there and really let the clients focus on the pixels. Let them focus on taking their time to make it look the way it needs to look, make it feel the way it needs to feel, making sure that user experience is great, and try to unify as much of the business logic as possible outside of the client, which saves time in some areas, takes a little longer in other areas. Again, if you plan for it, it can be done properly."

 📶 "Let the clients focus on the pixels" is the line I keep coming back to, because it gives the design and app teams back the work only they can do, how the thing feels on a 65-inch TV and on a phone on the bus, and it puts the rules that make money in one place where they get changed once. I also like that he names the cost, since some work gets slower and the payoff only comes if you decide it on day one, which is the exact decision most services skip when they are racing to get onto the next device.

 😎 Full disclosure, Mercury is a current client of A Guy With A Scarf.
The full episode is on the A Guy With A Scarf YouTube channel: https://lnkd.in/dqHguVBw
If your service runs on eight or more devices, where does your business logic live today, and how many copies of it are there?

 👉 If you want to see how Quicksilver Stream puts this into practice, ask Mercury for a demo here: https://lnkd.in/dNd9UC8R

Day one of Wave by Vento at OGR Torino, from the front row of Sala Fucine.
Tim Berners-Lee said out loud that he has no fix yet for what AI answers do to the click, the visit and the economics of publishing.
Jony Ive explained why the man who put multi-touch in every pocket gave the Ferrari Luce real analogue needles and physical controls, and admitted the launch reaction taught him that "you can make something new and different, that's rubbish, that's very easy".
Kalshi's Luana Lopes Lara told us CNN, Fox, CNBC and CBS now run her odds instead of polls.
Petar Veličković of Google DeepMind and Giorgio Chiellini agreed that a model can tell you a goal was likely and still cannot tell you why it happened, which is what coaches are paid for. Beeple brought a robot dog that squats and prints what it sees.
A strong lineup, and I wrote it all up with quotes and photos. I also wrote what made me uncomfortable as a Torinese: an opening that cast the Agnelli family as disruptors, a requested standing ovation for the host, a moderator from a paper his holding company owns, and reserved front rows while the press stood at the back. I stood up for Berners-Lee. As far as I could see, I was the only one.

▶️ A guy with a scarf NEW EPISODE
Could you run an in-house streaming platform without building every piece of it yourself, and swap an authentication, video or analytics vendor without touching a single client app?

🎙️ That is the question behind my conversation with Stephen Tallent, who founded Mercury Intermedia in 1996 and carries the CEO and CTO roles together. Mercury is a client of mine, so read this with that in mind, and I can vouch for what I saw on screen and what he said on the record.

1️⃣ Control of the endpoints your apps talk to. Stephen prefers the word control to ownership, and Quicksilver Stream keeps the business logic in one set of APIs so the apps can "focus on the pixels". His example is an authentication SDK dropped into every client app, which saves time on day one and lands the change in every app at once the day that vendor gets acquired.
2️⃣ No lock-in, including to Mercury. I challenged a vendor for saying it, and his answer was "if you provide a good product and you provide good service, they're gonna stay with you whether they have to or not". Customers keep their data, can swap any piece of the stack and can bring development in-house, which Stephen says a dozen customers have done with Mercury. He also named the tension himself: the customer needs control and the vendor needs to make money.
3️⃣ A producer builds a page by asking for it, no box-ticking and menu-scrolling. In the demo I described a feature I wanted, a producer testing a new page layout in plain language, and the team did it in front of me on the working platform. I had thought my idea was clever and it already existed, so I felt a mix of embarrassment and surprise.
One of the most clever use of AI I have seen in a B2B product so far. Great news for streaming platform producer teams.

What intrigued me about Quicksilver Stream is that it is not yet-another-streaming-platform. It sits between the client apps and the vendors a customer chooses, so video platform, or an authentication provider can change underneath it.
This conversation exists because the Mercury team read two of my articles, and one sentence in the second, "the stack is the product", led to a phone call with Tom Richardson, some strategy work together and now this interview. I write nearly every day and rarely see where a piece ends up, so for anyone asking what writing on LinkedIn returns, this is one of the clearest answers I have.

The full conversation, with the quotes and three questions to take to your own architecture, is in the article and YouTube video or Spotify podcast.

To see Quicksilver Stream, visit mercury.io and schedule a demo, and if you would like an introduction, write to me and tell me what you want to see.
Mike Ligon

posts.author: Carlo De Marchis
posts.text:
10 Things To Consider about the second Genius Sports CEO letter 📝
In March I wrote about Mark Locke's first letter, the one defending the $1.2 billion Legend deal. Seven months later there is a second one, "Americans are Going to Keep Wagering", and this time the subject is prediction markets. Same format, same footnotes, same forward-looking statements notice at the bottom, and the same audience: investors asking what happens to Genius if the courts or Congress take sports contracts away from Kalshi and Polymarket.

His point in one sentence 🎯 Americans will keep wagering on sport whatever the courts decide, and Genius gets paid however that wagering is routed, because it supplies the exchanges, the market makers behind them and the sportsbooks competing with them for the same customer. The rules decide who pays Genius; the demand, in his telling, guarantees that someone does.

The 🔟 things to consider:
1️⃣ It is an investor document that happens to be on LinkedIn, written while the Kalshi cases and the Supreme Court petition are still open.
2️⃣ The thesis separates the demand for wagering from the structure that carries it, and never describes a scenario in which Genius loses.
3️⃣ Settlement is where he is strongest: the Western Michigan at Michigan market on 5 September, $18.6 million paid out on a broadcast clock that had one second put back.
4️⃣ The economics claim, that an exchange dollar pays Genius as well as a sportsbook dollar, "match or exceed" in his words, has no public number under it.
5️⃣ Two Eilers & Krejcik percentages, 69 per cent and 2 per cent, carry the whole "net benefit" argument, and DraftKings and FanDuel read the same monitor.
6️⃣ The politics paragraph names Donald Trump Jr. and Stephanie Cutter in the same breath as a bipartisan bill to ban the contracts, which is more candid than the format usually allows.
7️⃣ Connecticut's subpoenas have two Genius entities on the list, and the letter gets past that in two sentences.
8️⃣ The February letter and this one are one argument in two parts, and Prediction.com launched two days later to prove it.
9️⃣ The timing tells you what the letter is for: after Q2, after the exchange deals, in the first NFL season with real exchange volume, built to be quoted back in a year.
🔟 What is missing: Sportradar, the leagues, the taxes already in force in Illinois and coming in North Carolina, and anywhere outside the US.

For paid members there is an appendix 📎 with the company timeline from Betgenius in 2001 to Prediction.com, four years of financials with the three 2026 guidance revisions side by side, the Legend deal terms, and a short Mark Locke bio built only on what I could source.

Do you buy the settlement argument, and would you believe "match or exceed" before seeing a number? Share what you think 👇

⚽ 🤖 FIFA wants fan journey tech for the Women’s World Cup 2027, next-generation wearables and connected substitution boards.

Earlier this year, at the Bundesliga SportsInnovation event in Düsseldorf, I shared a stage with Nicolas Evans from FIFA, talking 3D data, officiating and the Football Technology Centre, and what stayed with me was how much of FIFA's innovation work now runs through structured channels rather than conversations in a hospitality box.

This week those channels opened three new doors. The FIFA Innovation Programme has published three challenges:
⚽ Fan journey technology for the FIFA Women's World Cup 2027 in Brazil, which FIFA says is its first innovation challenge tied to a specific competition. Applications close on 1 November 2026, and the criteria ask for a fully operational solution already delivered across multiple projects, commercial partner integration and measurable ROI. Four weeks is short, but count backwards from kick-off on 24 June 2027 through FIFA's five-step process and there is little other room to deploy anything.
⚽ Next-generation sports wearables, measuring hydration, load, recovery and stress in real time. Working prototype minimum, no deadline, with validation through FIFA's research partners and academic institutions on offer.
⚽ Connected substitution boards, hardware that links to the substitution software FIFA already runs and shows player numbers to the stadium. Lightweight, durable, three hours of battery, manual fallback, working prototype minimum, no deadline.

All three go through the same portal, which runs on a video pitch platform, so expect to pitch on camera.

If you run fan journey, ticketing, accessibility or in-stadium technology that is already live with reputable clients, the Women's World Cup brief is written for you and the clock is running, so apply. If you build wearables or match operations hardware, the other two are open with no deadline, so get your prototype evidence in order and go. Know a company that fits one of the three? Tag them below.

And if you are preparing an application and want a second pair of eyes on the pitch, the positioning or the ROI story, message me.

Hat tip to Juan Iraola, whose post is where I first saw the announcement.

posts.text:
True story.
I was scrolling and my eyes immediately stopped on OTT.
Streaming. Obviously.
Except it wasn’t.
It was a monthly planner in Italian.
In Italian, the second half of the year goes:
GIU · LUG · AGO · SET · OTT · NOV · DIC
And OTT is simply ottobre. October.
It took my brain a few seconds to accept that nobody was talking about streaming.
Am I slightly biased and obsessed with streaming?
Possibly.
Happy OTT everyone.
